questions.question: Trace a repo rate increase through all five links of the transmission mechanism, ending with its effect on inflation, and name the side effect complete answers must mention.
questions.expected_answer: 1. The SARB raises the repo rate, so the commercial banks' own funding from the central bank costs more. 2. Banks recover this by lifting the prime lending rate. 3. Every loan priced off prime — bonds, vehicle finance, cards, overdrafts — becomes dearer. 4. Households and firms hold back on borrowing and spending. 5. Aggregate demand cools, sellers lose room to raise prices, and inflation eases back toward the 3-6% band. Side effect: the same tightening slows production and can cost jobs while it works, with indebted households feeling it first.

questions.question: A scenario states that the Minister of Finance adjusted the repo rate. Identify the error, explain why the separation of the two drivers matters, and give the sorting question that catches such errors.
questions.expected_answer: The repo rate is the instrument of the South African Reserve Bank, which is constitutionally independent — no minister or politician can move it. The minister's instruments are the Budget's spending and taxation. The separation matters because independence lets the Bank take unpopular anti-inflation decisions free of political pressure. The sorting question: 'whose hand is on the lever?' — the Reserve Bank's hand means monetary policy; the government's hand, through the Budget, means fiscal policy.

questions.question: State the method for labelling any policy move expansionary or contractionary, then classify: (a) an increase in social grants, (b) a rise in company tax, and (c) a cut in the repo rate.
questions.expected_answer: Ask whether the move adds spending power to the economy (expansionary) or withdraws it (contractionary). (a) Higher grants put money directly into households' pockets — expansionary fiscal policy. (b) A company tax rise withdraws spending power from firms — contractionary fiscal policy. (c) A repo cut makes borrowing cheaper and encourages spending — expansionary monetary policy.
